extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate liberal-arts students learning data visualization and data science (readers of the textbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for designing, critiquing, and understanding data visualizations with emphasis on truthfulness, perception, and pedagogy for liberal-arts students. Covers EDA techniques, Tufte's principles, uncertainty visualization, animation, and ethical/political implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical Excellence (Tufte)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical excellence is the well‑designed presentation of interesting data—a matter of substance, of statistics, and of design. Graphical excellence consists of complex ideas communicated with clarity, precision and efficiency. Graphical excellence is that which gives to the viewer the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time with the least ink in the smallest space. Graphical excellence is nearly always multivariate. And graphical excellence requires telling the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Tufte's principles as an overall design goal: prioritize substance over ornament, present many numbers coherently in a small space, encourage comparison, and integrate the graphic with statistical and verbal descriptions. The quoted principles should guide tradeoffs about ink, space, and information density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth / Avoid deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical displays must 'tell the truth' and designers have responsibility as arbiters of facts and educators; poor design can misinform or be used to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of how ordering, axes, scales, and decorative choices can hide or distort facts. Examples: the Challenger O‑ring display (poor arrangement hid the temperature relationship) and 'Sharpie‑gate' (altered map) illustrate harms. Prioritize honest representation over persuasive or self‑promoting presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present uncertainty clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: A major challenge is conveying uncertainty in a way people readily understand (e.g., cone of uncertainty vs distribution of possible tracks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techniques such as showing distributions of possible outcomes, hypothetical outcome plots, spaghetti plots with fading, or animated distributions rather than relying solely on error bars. Consider which representation best communicates the degree and nature of uncertainty to the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for perception and audience understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Design should begin with perception and understanding (the consumer) as well as design values (the producer); ask: when you see a graph, what do you notice, what do you wonder, and what is the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor visuals to how your audience perceives and interprets visual elements. Consider glanceability (peripheral attention), cognitive load, and what questions viewers will ask. Use ordering, emphasis, and annotation to guide the viewer to the intended inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chartjunk / unnecessary decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Poorly designed graphs—'chartjunk'—distract, confuse, and can mislead; graphs should serve a clear purpose (description, exploration, tabulation, or decoration) and avoid extraneous ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove noninformative ink and decorative elements that do not aid interpretation. Ensure every visual element has a purpose related to clarity or data communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate arrangement and ordering to reveal patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing how to lay out and order data (e.g., arranging launches by liftoff temperature rather than liftoff date) can reveal relationships that poor arrangements obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternate orderings, groupings, and encodings that make relevant relationships visible. Reorder axes or facets to highlight covariation rather than chronological or arbitrary orderings when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploratory Data Analysis practices (Tukey)
rubrics_metrics.description: EDA emphasizes descriptive and exploratory approaches: tallying, stem-and-leaf displays for small counts, box plots for group comparisons, thoughtful transformations to uncover linear trends, and examining residuals to find where trends do not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, robust displays for initial exploration (stem-and-leaf, boxplots, scatterplots). Transform variables to reveal structure and inspect residuals to diagnose model inadequacy. Treat visualization as an iterative exploration tool, not just final presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate graphical, statistical, and verbal descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphs should be closely integrated with the statistical and verbal descriptions of a data set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present visuals in isolation. Provide concise captions, annotations, and linked statistical summaries so the graphic and text jointly support understanding and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor multivariate displays when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical excellence is nearly always multivariate—good displays often present multiple dimensions of information simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, encode multiple variables (e.g., via color, size, facets, animation) to convey richer relationships, but balance multivariate encoding against perceptual limits and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use animation carefully to show time and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Animated displays bring time into visualization and can convey unfolding structure or uncertainty (e.g., Gapminder, Periscopic examples), but they can also induce anxiety or distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animation to reveal temporal dynamics or sampling variability; ensure controls, pacing, and visual persistence support comprehension. Consider whether a static small‑multiples layout might better support accurate comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground encoding choices in empirical graphical perception research
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose visual encodings based on empirical work (e.g., Cleveland & McGill) about what perceptual mappings are most accurate and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer position and length encodings for quantitative comparisons over less accurate encodings (e.g., area, color hue) when precise comparisons are needed. Consult empirical studies when selecting encodings for specific tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of psychological affordances and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some creative encodings (e.g., Chernoff faces) exploit psychological sensitivities (faces) but may not succeed; designers must question whether such displays truly aid interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novel or metaphorical encodings empirically or by user testing. Avoid relying on intuitions about perception without testing; be mindful of cultural/contextual interpretations (e.g., facial features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and civic responsibility in visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: As leaders, arbiters of facts, and educators, data visualizers have ethical obligations: better graphs foster a better informed citizenry; poor visualizations can endanger lives or mislead public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider downstream societal effects of how data are presented. Prioritize clarity, fairness, and accessibility; disclose limitations and uncertainty; avoid persuasive misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique heuristics / ask diagnostic questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a graph, ask directed questions: What does the graph tell you at a glance? What does it actually say on inspection? How could you improve it to make content more informative about its title? Why was it designed this way? Does it matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist when reviewing or teaching visualization: assess initial impressions, detailed accuracy, possible redesigns, designer motivations, and importance of any flaws.
